extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in healthcare policy, pharmaceutical pricing, and congressional oversight
extracted.subtask_description: A news report covering a congressional oversight hearing into a pharmaceutical company's EpiPen pricing and related corporate practices, focusing on CEO testimony, pricing justification, market dominance, and regulatory/antitrust concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a clear justification for price increases
rubrics_metrics.description: Executives should give a reason for increases in product prices; unexplained hikes ('jacked up the price ... for no discernible reason') produce public and congressional outrage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When questioned, companies should present the rationale and evidence behind price changes (cost drivers, R&D, market factors). Failure to do so invites intense scrutiny and political criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and candor in testimony and financial disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress expects candid, honest, and professionally presented financial information; 'these dumbed-down versions do not make sense without the definitions' and actions that 'feel like you are not being candid and honest with Congress' are unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide detailed profit-and-loss breakdowns with definitions for line items, include supply-chain/payment details (e.g., payments to pharmacy benefit managers), and respond promptly to requests for supporting data (e.g., commit to providing missing information within a specified timeframe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain profit margins and cost accounting
rubrics_metrics.description: When asserting a specific profit per unit (e.g., 'Mylan makes a profit of $50 per EpiPen'), companies should explain what is included in 'costs' and whether categories such as sales, marketing, disease awareness, access programs, and R&D are counted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify whether R&D is included, distinguish direct product costs from broader corporate expenses, and be prepared to justify how profit-per-unit figures were calculated to avoid accusations of obfuscation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid anticompetitive agreements in access programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs that provide discounted or free product to institutions (e.g., schools) but include provisions that schools 'would not buy competitive products' raise antitrust concerns and can prompt investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design access/discount programs without exclusivity clauses that prevent purchasers from buying competitors' products; be prepared for regulatory scrutiny if exclusivity or market-foreclosing practices are alleged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase availability and patient access as part of corporate response
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies should take tangible steps to improve availability and affordability (e.g., free products to qualifying families, increased coupon amounts) to address public anger over pricing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Access measures should be substantive and targeted (e.g., free supply for low-income families, expanded coupons for insured patients). Note that such measures may be seen as insufficient if broader pricing or market power issues remain unaddressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote market competition but recognize its limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress and witnesses often call for more competition to drive down prices, but the introduction of alternatives does not always lower prices (example: Auvi-Q's 2013 introduction did not reduce prices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies intended to increase competition should consider barriers to entry, market dynamics, and whether mere availability of alternatives is sufficient to produce price reductions; regulators may pursue both competition policy and investigations where market power is suspected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsiveness to oversight and readiness for public accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies summoned to testify should expect public shaming and aggressive questioning; some members used allotted time for public reprimand rather than questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare for both technical interrogation and reputational attacks; provide thorough preparation for testimony, anticipate pointed public criticism, and have strategies to address both factual and reputational concerns.
